title: Employee & Department Inner Join
question: How do you write a query to retrieve all columns from the employees and departments tables where the department_id matches?

options.text: SELECT * FROM employees INNER JOIN departments ON employees.department_id = departments.department_id;
SELECT * FROM employees JOIN departments WHERE employees.department_id = departments.department_id;
SELECT * FROM employees LEFT JOIN departments ON employees.department_id = departments.department_id;

explanation: INNER JOIN returns only matching rows across both tables on department_id.

title: Filtering Aggregated Salaries
question: Which SQL query finds the average salary for each department, but only includes departments with an average salary greater than 50,000?

options.text: SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE AVG(salary) > 50000 GROUP BY department_id;
SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000;
SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id WHERE AVG(salary) > 50000;
SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) FROM employees HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000 GROUP BY department_id;

explanation: The HAVING clause filters group results after aggregation (AVG).

title: Subquery Comparison
question: Which SQL query retrieves all employees whose salary is greater than the overall average salary?

options.text: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees);
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > AVG(salary);
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary > ALL (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees);
SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary IN (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees);

explanation: A subquery computes the aggregate average before comparing against individual employee rows.

title: Department Headcount
question: Which SQL statement will count the total number of employees in each department?

options.text: SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees;
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;
SELECT COUNT(department_id) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;
SELECT department_id, COUNT(department_id) FROM employees;

explanation: GROUP BY department_id is required when selecting non-aggregated column department_id with COUNT(*).

title: Orders & Customers Linking
question: How would you write a query to combine rows from orders and customers where customer_id matches?

options.text: SELECT * FROM orders INNER JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.customer_id;
SELECT * FROM orders JOIN customers WHERE orders.customer_id = customers.customer_id;
SELECT * FROM orders LEFT JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.customer_id;
SELECT * FROM orders RIGHT JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.customer_id;

explanation: INNER JOIN with an explicit ON clause is standard SQL syntax.

title: Sales per Category (Including Zero Sales)
question: How would you find total sales per product category, INCLUDING categories without any order items?

options.text: SELECT products.product_category_name, SUM(order_items.price) FROM orders RIGHT JOIN order_items ON orders.order_id = order_items.order_id RIGHT JOIN products ON order_items.product_id = products.product_id GROUP BY products.product_category_name;
SELECT products.product_category_name, SUM(order_items.price) FROM orders JOIN order_items USING(order_id) JOIN products USING(product_id) GROUP BY products.product_category_name;

SELECT products.product_category_name, SUM(order_items.price) FROM products LEFT JOIN order_items ON products.product_id = order_items.product_id LEFT JOIN orders ON order_items.order_id = orders.order_id GROUP BY products.product_category_name;

SELECT products.product_category_name, SUM(order_items.price) FROM orders INNER JOIN order_items ON orders.order_id = order_items.order_id INNER JOIN products ON order_items.product_id = products.product_id GROUP BY products.product_category_name;

explanation: Starting from products table with LEFT JOIN preserves all product categories even when sales are NULL.

title: The Algiers Scenario: Code Review & Refactoring
question: Analyze the query designed to return "the order value of every Algiers user's 2nd completed order". Point out the logical flaws and provide a corrected SQL query.
buggySql:
WITH RankedOrders AS (
    SELECT u.user_id, o.order_id, o.order_value, o.order_status,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY o.order_timestamp ASC) AS order_sequence
    FROM users u JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
    WHERE u.city = 'Algiers' 
)
SELECT user_id, order_id, order_value FROM RankedOrders
WHERE order_sequence = 2 AND order_status = 'completed';
correctSql:
WITH RankedOrders AS (
    SELECT u.user_id, o.order_value,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY u.user_id 
        ORDER BY o.order_timestamp ASC
    ) AS order_sequence
    FROM users u
    JOIN orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id
    WHERE u.city = 'Algiers' 
      AND o.order_status = 'completed'
)
SELECT user_id, order_value
FROM RankedOrders WHERE order_sequence = 2;
explanation: Two bugs: (1) no PARTITION BY user_id, so numbering runs across all Algiers users instead of per-user; (2) filtering order_status after ranking means the '2nd row' may not even be a completed order — the status filter must happen before ranking.

title: Active Users without Cancelled Orders
question: Which query selects users who placed orders, but NEVER had a single order with order_status = "cancelled"?

options.text: SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE order_status != "cancelled";
SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM orders WHERE user_id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders WHERE order_status = "cancelled");
SELECT user_id FROM orders GROUP BY user_id HAVING order_status != "cancelled";
SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM orders WHERE order_status IS NULL;

explanation: Option B excludes any user_id that appears in the list of users with at least one cancelled order.

title: Wallet Balance Running Total
question: Which Window Function clause calculates a running total sum of transaction amounts ordered by created_at?

options.text: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY created_at ASC)
SUM(amount) GROUP BY created_at
RUNNING_SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY created_at)
CUMULATIVE(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY transaction_id)

explanation: SUM() combined with OVER (ORDER BY created_at) produces an unbounded preceding running total.

title: Driver Rating Percentile Ranking
question: To find the top 10% highest rated drivers per city, which window function is best suited?

options.text: DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY rating DESC)
NTILE(10) OVER (PARTITION BY city ORDER BY rating DESC)
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY rating DESC)
COUNT(rating) OVER (PARTITION BY city)

explanation: NTILE(10) splits rows into 10 equal buckets per city, where bucket 1 represents the top 10% percentile.

title: Finding Duplicate Orders
question: How do you check if there are duplicate order_ids in the order_items table?

options.text: SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
SELECT order_id FROM order_items WHERE COUNT(order_id) > 1;
SELECT DISTINCT order_id FROM order_items WHERE order_id IS DUPLICATE;
SELECT order_id, SUM(order_item_id) FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id;

explanation: GROUP BY order_id paired with HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 surfaces order_ids that repeat more than once.
